talks.title: 02 - 0x0E - Adaptive Adversaries
talks.teaser: Examines 02 - 0x0E - Adaptive Adversaries and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Overview: Dave Kennedy, founder of TrustedSec and Binary Defense, presents at BruCON on adaptive adversaries and how offense and defense have evolved over 15 years of technological change.

Key Topics: How adversaries adapt to improved defensive visibility; the evolution from simple attacks to sophisticated operations; Kennedy's background including Mr. Robot consulting and media appearances; and building tools that improve the industry.

Technical Details: Kennedy contrasts security challenges from 10-15 years ago with today's environment of better visibility and more capable adversaries. He discusses how attackers adapt their techniques as defenses improve, requiring continuous evolution.

Takeaways: Adversaries continuously adapt to defensive improvements. Security programs must evolve beyond static controls and embrace adaptive defense strategies informed by current threat intelligence.

talks.title: 03 - 0x0E - I am become loadbalancer, owner of your network
talks.teaser: Investigates 03 - 0x0E - practitioners am become loadbalancer, owner of your network and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Overview:
Nate Warfield, Director of Research at Eclypsium, co-founder of the CTI League, and former F5 engineer of ten years, provides an in-depth examination of post-exploitation techniques on F5 BIG-IP load balancers. Drawing upon a decade of internal engineering experience and extensive incident response investigations, Warfield discusses how network edge devices serve as prime persistence platforms for sophisticated threat actors such as UNC3524. The presentation explores the internal dual-plane architecture of BIG-IP, management interface exposure flaws, plaintext key storage, and methods for weaponizing native subsystem utilities to maintain covert network control.

Key Topics:
- History of F5 BIG-IP vulnerabilities (hardcoded ISO SSH keys, directory traversals, JSON REST RCEs)
- Threat actor UNC3524 tradecraft analysis, persistence methods, and operational shortcomings
- BIG-IP system architecture: proprietary TMOS/TMM traffic plane versus CentOS management plane
- Post-exploitation methodologies: credential/TLS key harvesting, peer device discovery, and covert persistence

Technical Details:
Warfield reviews historical high-severity flaws in F5 BIG-IP appliances, beginning with an early vulnerability where an SSH keypair was hardcoded in ISO distribution images due to failing key-rotation scripts. He covers path traversal flaws (including the 2020 vulnerability utilizing `..;/` sequences as previously researched by Orange Tsai) and the 2022 JSON REST API exploit capable of fitting within a single tweet. He analyzes Mandiant's report on UNC3524, an advanced cyber espionage group that remained undetected in victim networks for 18 months via SAN arrays and load balancers. Warfield critiques UNC3524's tradecraft: the actors installed a modified Dropbear SSH client with hardcoded passwords and fragile RC script modifications, lacking reliable persistence across reboots or software upgrades and forcing them to drop supplementary web shells on internal servers.

Explaining the underlying architecture, Warfield contrasts BIG-IP's proprietary Traffic Management Operating System (TMOS/TMM)—which controls network interfaces and executes real-time packet inspection via embedded TCL/TK iRules—with the management plane running CentOS Linux. While administrators assume management interfaces are isolated out-of-band, F5 historically enabled administrative access by default across Self-IP addresses on data-plane interfaces, exposing management endpoints to external scanning. Once root access is achieved, BIG-IP serves as an ideal persistence environment: appliances feature large storage capacities, lack endpoint detection and response (EDR) agents or AV monitoring, and retain full CentOS utilities (albeit with Python 2 and removed compilers). Attackers can harvest plaintext TLS certificates and private keys stored under `/config/`, decode `BIGipServer` cookies via Shodan to map backend server IPs and cleartext HTTP ports, and query native cluster commands to uncover peering appliances, internal subnets, and routing topology. Low-level configuration changes or backdoor listeners on the CentOS management plane operate invisibly to operators, evading load-balancing configuration synchronization alarms.

Key Takeaways:
Enterprise perimeter load balancers represent critical operational blind spots because they function as unmonitored black boxes lacking standard EDR telemetry. Security teams must audit Self-IP configurations to verify that administrative management services (HTTPS and SSH) are strictly disabled on data-plane interfaces. Defenders and incident responders must monitor the integrity of `/config/` directories, inspect underlying boot partitions and startup scripts, and deploy network segmentation to isolate appliance management interfaces from internal and external traffic.

talks.title: 04 - 0x0E - DNS as Criticial Infrastructure - do youknow where your domain is ?
talks.teaser: Presents 04 - 0x0E - DNS as Criticial Infrastructure - do youknow where your domain is and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
DNS as Foundational Infrastructure

A 32-year Internet veteran and longtime DNS educator argues “it wasn’t DNS—it was DNS” reflects reality: when DNS breaks, TLS validation, failover, load balancing, and countless services fail. Yet DNS remains a curriculum footnote despite underappreciated fragility at global and national scales.

Resiliency Best Practices

Classic guidance—geographically separate authoritative servers, diverse ASNs/IPv4 blocks, avoid co-located hypervisor DNS pairs—is well documented (e.g., BIND operators guides) but unevenly deployed. The speaker reverse-engineered public DNS without full zone data, painting broad strokes over six months of snapshots with little improvement.

Research Origin

Work began during COVID-era surveys of Norwegian .no domains for DNSSEC uptake (strong due to registrar defaults), expanding into ccTLD diversity and whether operators follow recommended resilience patterns. Imperfect measurement still reveals systemic concentration and misconfiguration risks.

Operational Mindset

The talk urges packet-level literacy (tcpdump over application lies), CLI tooling including jq for JSON DNS data, and treating DNS like critical national infrastructure worthy of deep operational expertise—not assumed background magic.

talks.title: 05-BruCON 0x0E -A Black-Box Security Evaluation of the SpaceX Starlink User Terminal-Lennert Wouters
talks.teaser: Outlines 05-BruCON 0x0E -A Black-Box Security Evaluation of the SpaceX Starlink User Terminal-Lennert Wouters and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Starlink architecture

Lennert Wouters explains Starlink's space and earth segments: LEO satellites with laser links, user terminals, and ground gateways connected to the internet. Because SpaceX would not provide hardware for research, his team bought a consumer terminal—the practical attack surface for satellite access.

Prior work and hardware variants

He surveys teardown and analysis by Mike on Space, SignalPad, Calling Offline, Wi-Fi router reverse engineering, and Dan Murray's rectangular terminal work. SpaceX shipped many circular, rectangular, high-performance, and transceiver revisions with different STMicro Gatson SoC silicon versions.

Teardown findings

Opening the dish exposes PoE, motor, and an unpopulated UART that prints u-boot output but ignores input. A development login prompt appears only on dev hardware. Removing the metal shield reveals GPS, clocking, PoE, and a custom quad-core Arm SoC plus secure element, eMMC, DDR3, and resistor-encoded hardware revision IDs.

RF silicon

The phased array uses STMicro Shiraz beamformers and Pulsar front-end modules; decapped die images were published after sending chips to John McMaster.
